newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Unichem targets retail, Europe.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Unichem targets retail, Europe.

text.p: Britain's Unichem Plc said on Wednesday that it was targeting rapid growth in its retail pharmacy chain and the expansion of its drug wholesaling business in Europe.

In a telephone interview with Reuters, chief executive Jeffrey Harris said its year-long, losing battle with Germany's Gehe AG for control of Lloyds Chemists Plc had been a distraction, but added "we survived in very good shape."
"Despite the fact that we lost Lloyds, which was clearly a disappointment, we think there is a huge number of opportunities for us in the healthcare market," Harris said.

Earlier, Unichem said the tussle for Lloyds, which it finally lost in January, had cost it a net 13.2 million stg in fees, commissions and costs, causing pre-tax profit to slide 18 percent to 40.3 million stg. Without the bid costs, pre-tax profit rose 8.3 percent to 53.5 million stg. Sales rose 5.4 percent to 1.48 billion stg.
Harris said the wholesale operation, whose sales rose 5.1 percent to 1.33 billion stg last year, had started 1997 well, with like-for like sales up 10 percent in January and February.
"We are picking up market share," he said, adding that Unichem was able to benefit from Gehe's "indigestion as it rationalises."

He said the attempt to gain control of Lloyds, and its 900 strong chain of chemists shops, was "a significant distraction. We tried to confine that...but it does have an effect on the business. However that is now past and we are looking to see what opportunities we can take."

Harris said the group's goal was to add 100 pharmacies to its chain of 459 stores this year, although this would be done on a "piecemeal basis". He said many more pharmacies were coming on to the market now that the Lloyds issue was settled.
Unichem also wants to expand its wholesaling presence in Europe, which is currently limited to Portugal.
Harris said the company wanted to "restructure relationships" with a network of partners across Europe, and said this could happen through cross shareholdings, mergers and acquisitions.

"The challenge now is to try to make a loose combinaiton into a more cohesive group," said Harris, although he added that this "takes lot of time. We are a cautious management." He also declined to say which European countries Unichem was targetting.
Harris also takes a sanguine view of a possible change of government in Britain after the May 1 election, despite the key role that health is likely to play in the political fight.

"We have done a lot of lobbying with Labour and our view is that there will be fewer changes than one might have expected," he said. Harris noted that an existing government discussion document on the future of health provision by pharmacies had survived in parliament.

Although stripped of highly controversial proposals, which would have allowed pharmacies to provide doctor's services, he said this would still allow pharmacies to take much of the workload from doctors in areas like basic diagnosis and cholesterlol testing.

He said Labour, which is currently well ahead of the ruling Conservatives in opinion polls, did not seem anxious to change the Pharmaceutical Price Regulation Scheme, which controls the price of drugs supplied the British government, and also seemed "more interested in retaining" the Retail Price Maintenance (RPM) scheme for over-the-counter medicines.
The threat of abolishing RPM met a howl of protest from independent chemists, although Harris said abolition would have a "trivial" impact on Unichem.
